planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Daisy's compact habit and heavy flowering make it well suited to foundation plantings and smaller borders where full-sized gardenias would eventually crowd the space.

directions: Daisy stands apart from most garden gardenias by producing flat, single, daisy-like flowers about 2 inches across with a small yellow center rather than the dense double rosettes of cultivars like Aimee or Chuck Hayes, and it tends to flower more heavily over a long late-spring-to-early-fall season as a result. Give it full sun for the best bloom, though afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps prevent leaf scorch and bud drop. One of its most useful traits is resistance to root-knot nematodes, a soil pest that weakens and eventually kills many other gardenia cultivars in sandy Gulf Coast soils, making Daisy a good replacement choice where nematode damage has been a recurring problem. Keep soil consistently moist and strongly acidic and feed with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season to support its extended bloom cycle.
